paras: The whipping of Williams in Lee County, Georgia, was an attack in about June 1903 in which a committee of white farmers whipped a Black preacher from Columbus and ordered him to leave the county. The farmers blamed Williams for a wave of quitting and wage demands among Black servants and field hands, and the only known report, in the Americus Times-Recorder, treated the whipping as a deserved rebuke to a "walking delegate."

In the weeks before the attack, white employers throughout Lee County, south of Americus, had trouble keeping Black workers. Cooks, house girls, washerwomen and field hands quit, in many cases without warning, and many demanded higher wages before leaving. According to the Times-Recorder, it was "said" that this trouble came from the teachings of Williams, a preacher who advised strikes among Black workers.

A committee of farmers then "waited upon" Williams and whipped him with buggy traces, which the paper called a "buggy-trace ovation." They told him to return to his home in Columbus "as soon as he could travel," and the paper called the beating "about the severest thrashing one of his kind ever received." The report gives no date, no first name for Williams, and no names for the men who whipped him.
No report of arrests, of any official response, or of whether Williams left the county appears in the coverage.

The episode is known from one short item in the Americus Times-Recorder on June 20, 1903, under the headline "Waited Upon by a Committee" and the subhead "Colored Walking Delegate Is Roughly Handled." The paper borrowed the language of the labor movement, casting Williams as a "walking delegate" who was "stirring up strife," and it told the story from the employers' side, stressing that farmers had been "greatly inconvenienced." It presented the whipping as the response of white citizens who "resented his interference," with no account from Williams or the workers.
No other white paper and no Black newspaper is known to have reported the attack.

reader.title: Whipping of Williams in Lee County, Georgia
bases: A committee of farmers whipped a Black preacher and ordered him out of the county because he was said to have advised Black servants and field hands to quit and demand higher wages; the violence was aimed at Black labor action (A1).
Only one paper, the Americus Times-Recorder, reported the whipping, and its account of the cause rests on hearsay ('it is said') (A1).
